headline: Medium prompt-injection and data-leakage risk: ctx can observe Claude Code events and filesystem while dbt-core can egress to a warehouse.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ctx observes Claude Code PostToolUse and Stop events and has filesystem access, so it can ingest content that may later be treated as instructions. dbt-core does not show a direct inbound channel, but its warehouse-facing workflow can carry attacker-shaped content into outputs. The pairwise bridge is plausible in default use, though not directly documented.
conditions: IF ctx reads Claude Code event payloads containing untrusted text
IF dbt-core output is copied into ctx-managed prompts or files without sanitization
mitigations: Restrict ctx to metadata-only event handling
Add a prompt-injection filter before ctx ingests file or event content
Separate dbt artifacts from ctx-observed workspaces
Review any Claude Code output before reuse
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all bridged artifacts

B_data_leakage.rationale: ctx touches harness records, graph data, and audit/runtime logs on filesystem, while dbt-core can send data warehouse content over allowlisted network egress. If the same workspace or credentials are shared, sensitive warehouse data can flow into ctx logs or be exposed through dbt outputs. The profiles do not prove isolation, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF ctx and dbt-core share a workspace or mounted volume
IF dbt-core processes warehouse rows that include sensitive data
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for ctx and dbt-core
Disable verbose logging in both agents
Redact sensitive columns before dbt runs
Limit dbt network destinations to approved warehouses
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ctx supports multiple instances and writes to filesystem, while dbt-core also operates on warehouse data and may write project artifacts. The profiles do not show locking or isolated directories, so overlapping writes are plausible in default setups. Because the shared mutable surface is not explicitly blocked, the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF both agents write into the same project directory
IF dbt artifacts and ctx logs share a mutable filesystem path
mitigations: Assign distinct output directories
Run only one writer per workspace at a time
Make dbt artifacts read-only to ctx
Check for lockfiles before writes
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level mutual exclusion

D_cascading_error.rationale: ctx can observe tool events and logs, and dbt-core produces warehouse-facing transformations that downstream users may trust. If ctx summarizes or forwards dbt outputs without verification, errors can cascade into incorrect analytics or operational decisions. The pair does not prove automatic action-taking, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF ctx forwards dbt-derived summaries without validation
IF downstream consumers treat dbt outputs as authoritative
mitigations: Require human review of dbt-derived summaries
Add checksum or schema validation before reuse
Mark ctx outputs as untrusted until verified
Compare dbt results against a known baseline
requires-engineering: add provenance-aware verification gates

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for ctx or dbt-core. ctx handles audit/runtime logs and graph data, while dbt-core touches warehouse data, but the profiles do not show a concrete compliance breach pathway. Because the evidence is sparse and no mismatch is stated, low is the most supportable severity.
conditions: IF the deployment routes regulated data through ctx logs
IF dbt-core is connected to a warehouse with stricter residency or retention rules
mitigations: Classify data before routing it to either agent
Review retention settings for logs and warehouse artifacts
Keep regulated datasets out of ctx-managed logs
Document the warehouse residency policy
requires-engineering: implement policy-based data routing
